{{distinguish|Spatial heterogeneity}}

'''Spatial variability''' occurs when a quantity that is measured at different [[spatial location]]s exhibits values that differ across the locations.  Spatial variability can be assessed using [[spatial descriptive statistics]] such as the [[range (statistics)|range]].

Let us suppose that the Rev' z(x) is perfectly known at any point x within the field under study. Then the [[uncertainty]] about z(x) is reduced to zero, whereas its spatial variability still exists. Uncertainty is closely related to the amount of spatial variability, but it is also strongly dependent upon sampling.{{sfn | Delhomme | 1979 | pp=269–280}}

[[Geostatistics|Geostatistical]] analyses have been strictly performed to study the spatial variability of pesticide sorption{{sfn | Cambardella | Moorman | Novak | Parkin | 1994 | pp=1501–1511}}{{sfn | Novak | Moorman | Cambardella | 1997 | pp=1271–1277}}{{sfn|Jacques|Mouvet|Mohanty|Vereecken|1999|pp=31–52}} and degradation{{sfn |Price|Walker|Wood|Oliver|2001|pp=233–238}} in the field. Webster and Oliver{{sfn | Webster | 2007 | p=}} provided a description of geostatistical techniques. Describing uncertainty using geostatistics is not an activity exempt from uncertainty itself as [[variogram]] uncertainty may be large{{sfn | Jansen | 1998 | pp=247–253}} and [[spatial interpolation]] may be undertaken using different techniques.{{sfn | Dubus | Brown | Beulke | 2003 | pp=53–72}}
